title: The contract tool that "works well"
scenario:
You are a procurement manager at a food distributor. The buying team handles about 1,500 supplier contracts a year. A vendor offers an AI tool that summarises each contract for the buyers.

Your manager wants to sign after a one-week trial. You must write the acceptance criteria first. The exhibit shows the first draft and two notes from the legal team.
exhibit:
Contract summary tool: draft acceptance criteria (made-up example data)

Vendor claim: "96% accuracy on a public legal benchmark"

Draft criteria
  1. The tool should summarise contracts well.
  2. Summaries are safe.
  3. A summary is ready in under 30 seconds.
  4. Cost is under $0.40 per contract.

Notes from legal (estimates)
  Clumsy wording in a summary      a buyer spends ~2 minutes fixing it
  Missed auto-renewal clause       the company may pay for one more contract year
  Past contracts for testing       ~600 available, incl. 80 scanned PDFs

questions.prompt: Which draft criterion is the weakest acceptance test?

options.text: Criterion 3, because 30 seconds is too strict for a tool that reads long contracts.
options.explanation: Response time is a valid criterion in Anthropic's list (latency). It is specific and easy to measure from the tool log.

options.text: Criterion 1, because "well" is neither specific nor measurable, so nobody can pass or fail it.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's guide asks for specific, measurable criteria. Its bad example is "The model should classify sentiments well".

options.text: Criterion 4, because price is a purchasing question, not part of a quality test.
options.explanation: Anthropic's guide lists price as one of the common success criteria. Most use cases need several criteria, not quality alone.

options.text: Criteria 3 and 4, because only accuracy counts in an acceptance test for an AI tool.
options.explanation: The guide says most use cases need evaluation along several criteria, including latency and price.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite of criterion 2 fits Anthropic's guide best?

options.text: "Summaries are always fully safe and accurate, in every single case."
options.explanation: This is still not measurable. It names no test set, no check and no number.

options.text: "The vendor confirms in writing that the tool is safe to use for contracts."
options.explanation: A promise is not a test. Your criterion should say what you will measure on your own contracts.

options.text: "Buyers feel that the summaries are safe after the one-week trial."
options.explanation: A feeling is not a consistent scale. OpenAI's guide calls "it seems like it's working" a vibe-based eval.

options.text: "On 300 past contracts, no summary repeats a person's bank details."
options.explanation: Right. It is specific and measurable, like the guide's good safety example: a rate over a set number of trials.

questions.prompt: The vendor says: "96% on a public legal benchmark is above your 95% target, so you can skip your own test." What is the best reply?

options.text: Test it on our past contracts, mixed like our real work, including the 80 scanned PDFs.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's guide says to mirror your real task distribution and include edge cases. OpenAI's guide separates public benchmarks from tests of your own application.

options.text: Agree to sign: a public benchmark score is a stronger proof than a test that we write ourselves.
options.explanation: OpenAI's guide says benchmarks compare models in isolation. They don't show how the tool does on your contracts.

options.text: Ask the vendor for a score of 99% on the same benchmark before we sign the contract.
options.explanation: A higher score on someone else's tasks still says little about your supplier contracts.

options.text: Ignore accuracy and decide on the price per contract, because all benchmarks give the same result.
options.explanation: Quality still matters; the problem is only where it is measured. Test it on your own work.

questions.prompt: How should the criteria treat the two failure types in legal's notes?

options.text: Use one overall accuracy target, so every error counts the same and the test stays simple.
options.explanation: OpenAI's accuracy guide says to start with what a failure costs. A missed renewal clause costs far more than clumsy wording.

options.text: Launch first and count complaints for three months to learn which errors cost the most.
options.explanation: OpenAI's guide lists waiting until you ship before you write any evals as an anti-pattern.

options.text: Set a separate, stricter target for renewal clauses than for wording quality.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's guide says to know what a failure costs. Anthropic's example also sets a rule for how serious errors may be.

options.text: Leave wording out of the criteria, because a fix costs only about two minutes of work.
options.explanation: Cheap errors still matter if there are many of them. Give them a looser target, but keep them in the test.
